newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada settles Mulroney libel suit - report.
newsitem.headline: Canada settles Mulroney libel suit - report.

text.p: Former Prime Minister Brian Mulroney has reached an out-of-court settlement in his C$50 million ($37 million) libel lawsuit against the Canadian government, the Canadian Broadcasting Corp said on Sunday.

Citing a source close to the case, CBC television said the settlement included an "unequivocal apology" from the government for wrongly accusing Mulroney of taking kickbacks in Air Canada's $1.8 billion ($1.3 billion) purchase of Airbus Industrie jets in 1988.

Mulroney's lawsuit centered on a letter sent by Canada's Justice Department to Swiss authorities in September 1995 in which Mulroney was accused of accepting illegal commissions in the purchase of 34 Airbus A-320 aircraft.

The CBC said an official announcement of the settlement was to be made on Monday, the day the unprecendented lawsuit was scheduled to be heard in a Montreal court. In the settlement, the government also agreed to pay Mulroney's legal costs of about C$1 million ($740,000), the CBC said.
Government officials and Mulroney's legal team did not return reporters' telephone calls Sunday night.

In a pre-trial hearing in April 1996, Mulroney, who was Conservative prime minister from 1984 to 1993, vehemently denied the letter's allegations, accusing the Justice Department and Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) of "fascism" in their investigation of the Airbus matter.

In the 11-page letter sent to Swiss authorities, the Justice Department alleged secret commissions were paid to Mulroney, former Newfoundland Premier Frank Moores and businessman Karlheinz Schreiber in Air Canada's purchase of the Airbus jets. The carrier was owned by the Canadian government when it bought the aircraft.

The Justice Department had sent the letter to Swiss authorities to seek help in obtaining information about certain bank accounts in Switzerland. The letter accused Mulroney of taking part in a "conspiracy" to defraud the Canadian government by accepting kickbacks of up to C$4 million ($3 million).
On November, 18, 1995, the same day The Financial Post, a Toronto newspaper, published details of the Justice Deparment letter, Mulroney's lawyers said he would sue the government and RCMP.

In the pre-trial hearing in April 1996 Mulroney said all 31 allegations about him in the letter were "completely false." "I want justice and I want a court to say this is a massive libel against an innocent man," he said.

Legal observers said the libel suit was unprecedented in its scope and because of its political and legal implications. If the civil case proceeded, Mulroney and Canadian government officials were to face pointed questionning by lawyers during the up to 16 weeks scheduled for the trial.
"In matters like this, no one really comes up the winner," said Simon Chester, a Toronto lawyer specializing in libel law.

Mulroney's legal team planned to call 30 witnesses, including several senior government officials and Canada's justice minister. There was also speculation that former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and former U.S. President George Bush would be called as character witnesses for Mulroney.
